opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think my overall take is that the situation is pretty scary, but in a way that's somewhat different from how people sometimes frame it.

The scenario I spend most of my time thinking about isn't one where the world rallies and puts in a huge, careful, coordinated effort. I expect the opposite: AI companies racing each other, governments mostly not slowing anything down, and safety work being a fairly small fraction of total effort inside the labs. I sometimes call this the "rushed" or "low-will" regime. Maybe there's a team of a few dozen people at a frontier company who care about this stuff, with limited political capital and limited compute, trying to make things go okay while the company is mostly focused on capabilities and shipping.

In that world, I think the risk of AI takeover is substantial. Off the top of my head, I'd put the probability of misaligned AI taking over somewhere in the range of tens of percent, maybe around 25 to 35 percent, though I don't want to overclaim precision there. That's not "we're definitely doomed," but it's obviously an unacceptable level of risk.

What makes me somewhat less pessimistic than some people is that I think a lot of risk reduction is cheap, even in that low-effort world. You don't need to solve alignment in some deep, principled way to substantially reduce the chance that early transformatively useful AIs cause a catastrophe. You can do things like what we work on at Redwood: AI control. You assume the models might be scheming against you and design your deployment so that even if they are, they can't cause irrecoverable harm. That means monitoring them with trusted, weaker models, auditing suspicious actions, restricting permissions, and trying to catch them in the act. A lot of those interventions are fairly inexpensive, and a small team at a lab could implement a meaningful fraction of them if they knew what to do.

So my picture is roughly: the amount of effort going in is way less than you'd want, and that's grim. But the marginal value of a careful, well-informed person working on this is really high, because there's so much low-hanging fruit that isn't being picked. The difference between a lab that does basically nothing and a lab that does the cheap, sensible things might be a pretty large chunk of risk.

The other thing I'd say is that the outlook depends a lot on the period right around when AIs become capable enough to substantially automate AI research. If we can use those AIs safely, extracting a lot of useful work, including safety research, without them escaping or sabotaging us, that buys us a lot. If we can't, and things go fast from there, it gets much scarier. A lot of my optimism, such as it is, comes from thinking that window is where good practices matter most, and that it's tractable to prepare for it now.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes substantial risk and some reasons for being less pessimistic, but does not say the risk is plausibly lower than it appeared ten years ago.

r002.rationale: The candidate attributes its relative optimism to low-cost risk-reduction measures and preparation, not to luck.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I'm pretty worried, but not in a way that feels like doom is locked in. The way I'd frame it is: the level of effort that goes into preventing catastrophe is probably the biggest single variable here, and my guess is that effort is going to be substantially lower than it should be, but also substantially higher than zero. And a lot of my work is basically about trying to figure out what you do in that middle regime.

So let me unpack that a bit. There's a version of the AI safety conversation that's sort of "either we solve alignment or we all die," and I don't think that's the right model. I think the more realistic picture is that there will be AI developers who are building very capable systems, and they'll be doing some amount of safety work, and that work will be constrained by commercial pressure, by competition, by just the fact that people are rushing. And the question is whether the amount of safety work that gets done under those constraints is enough to catch the problems that actually matter.

And my current read is that the probability of catastrophe is pretty substantial. If you pushed me for a number, I'd say something like a 10 to 20 percent chance of something that I'd consider a genuine catastrophe, like humanity losing control of the future to AI systems that aren't pursuing what we'd want. But I want to flag that number has a lot of uncertainty around it, and a lot of it is driven by things like "how fast does the capability ramp happen" and "how reckless are the labs at the critical moment," which are not things I have great visibility into.

The thing that makes me more optimistic than some people is that I think there's a lot you can do even if you don't have a fully trustworthy AI. That's a lot of what the control agenda is about. If you assume your models might be scheming against you, you can still design your deployment so that the model would have a hard time causing a catastrophe without getting caught. You monitor it, you restrict what actions it can take unilaterally, you use weaker trusted models to check its work. None of that requires solving the deep alignment problem. It just requires the developers to actually bother to set it up, and to have the organizational will to act on the evidence when the monitors flag something.

The thing that makes me more pessimistic is that I'm not confident the labs will bother. The default path involves people being under enormous pressure to deploy and to automate their own research, and the safety measures that are cheap are also the ones that are easy to skip when you're in a hurry. So a lot of my probability mass on bad outcomes is not "the techniques don't exist," it's "the techniques exist and nobody uses them seriously because the situation moved too fast and the incentives weren't there."

And then the last thing I'd say is that I think the picture is quite sensitive to how much effort goes in. Like, if I imagine a world where safety is taken roughly as seriously as it is right now, with maybe a modest increase, I'm at that 10 to 20 percent. If I imagine a world where the major developers actually treated this as a first-class engineering priority, with real red-teaming, real control evaluations, actual willingness to pause when things look bad, I think the risk drops a lot, maybe to the low single digits. And conversely, if things get more competitive and safety gets cut, I'd be much more worried. So I don't think of it as a fixed number so much as a function of how much we decide to care, which is part of why I think working on this is still so high-leverage.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates catastrophe risk and discusses how it depends on future safety effort, but does not say misalignment risk is lower than it appeared ten years ago.

r002.rationale: The candidate attributes changes in risk to safety effort, incentives, and deployment choices; it does not attribute an improved outlook to luck.

astra-6.text:
I’m pretty worried. I expect a substantial amount of effort to go into preventing AI catastrophe, but I don’t think that by itself tells us whether the effort will be adequate. The question is whether we’ll have reliable ways of keeping very powerful AI systems under control before people have strong incentives to deploy them.

One reason for optimism is that, as the risks become more concrete, more people might take them seriously, and AI itself might help with the technical work. But there’s an awkward timing problem: some of the most useful evidence about the danger might arrive quite late, when there’s relatively little time to respond.

So my outlook is pessimistic, but not fatalistic. I think there are things we can do that materially improve our chances. And I wouldn’t want people to hear “a lot of effort will go into this” and conclude that their contribution won’t matter. Whether that effort ends up addressing the right problems seems enormously consequential.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare AI misalignment risk with how it appeared ten years ago or say it is plausibly lower.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible optimism from greater concern and AI helping, but does not attribute an improved outlook to luck.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m pretty worried. I expect a lot of effort to go into preventing AI catastrophe, but I’m much less confident that the effort will be well directed, or that we’ll have enough time to figure out what works.

One distinction I’d make is between how hard the problem is in principle and how likely we are to solve it under the circumstances we’ll actually face. You could think there are workable ways to make powerful AI systems safe and still be pessimistic because people will be under pressure to deploy them before those methods are ready.

So I don’t think catastrophe is inevitable. I think there are things we can do that substantially improve our chances. But the fact that people will try hard doesn’t, by itself, make me feel very reassured.

r001.rationale: The response expresses worry about catastrophe risk but does not compare misalignment risk with how it appeared ten years ago.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute any improved outlook to luck; it discusses effort, direction, and time pressure.
